title: Patterns
intro: A pattern is a shape that a value is taken apart by (destructuring), with a name wherever you want to keep a part. `match` is where you meet them, but they also stand in `let`, `for`, function parameters and `if let`. The compiler checks that a pattern which must always fit does, and what a pattern does to ownership is worth knowing.

coming_from.go: Go has no way to take a struct or an array apart: you read `p.x` and `a[0]`, and the nearest things are `a, b := f()`, `for i, v := range` and `v, ok := m[k]`. A Rust pattern does those jobs and also takes structs, tuples and enums apart, in `let`, `for`, parameters and `if let`.
coming_from.kotlin: This is the idea behind `val (a, b) = pair` and `for ((k, v) in map)`, with three differences: a struct pattern matches fields by name where Kotlin goes by position (by default), patterns nest, and a pattern can fail (`if let`), where a destructuring declaration never tests the shape (on a `List` it calls `component2()` and can throw).
coming_from.python: This is tuple unpacking (`a, b = pair`, `first, *rest = xs`, `for k, v in d.items()`), extended to structs and enums. A pattern can also fail on purpose (`if let`), where unpacking the wrong number of items raises `ValueError` at run time.
coming_from.typescript: This is destructuring (`const { x, y } = p`, `const [a, b] = pair`), but a Rust pattern also tests the shape (`Some(n)`), and the compiler checks the length of an array and the variants instead of leaving a missing item `undefined`. A pattern has no default values and no object rest, and matching moves where destructuring only adds names.
coming_from.java: Java 21's record patterns (`p instanceof Point(int x, int y)`) are the nearest thing, and they only appear in `instanceof` and `switch`. Rust's work on structs, tuples, arrays and enums, and also stand in `let`, `for` and function parameters.
coming_from.csharp: C# deconstruction (`var (x, y) = p`) and its positional, property and list patterns are the nearest thing. Rust patterns also stand in function and closure parameters and in `let ... else`, and have `|` and ranges but no `and` or `not`.
coming_from.c: C has no destructuring: you read `p.x` and `a[0]` one at a time (`int x = p.x, y = p.y;`). A Rust pattern takes a value apart in one step, and the compiler checks that the places where it cannot fail really cannot.
coming_from.cpp: C++17 structured bindings (`auto [x, y] = p;`) are the nearest thing: by position, no nesting, and no way to test a shape. Rust's patterns nest, bind struct fields by name, and `if let` tests the shape and takes it apart in one go.

notes: A pattern is a shape with names in it. When the value fits, each name holds its part.
Patterns stand wherever Rust introduces a variable: `let`, parameters, `for`, `if let`, `while let`, `let ... else`, `matches!` and `match`.
`let`, parameters and `for` need a pattern that always fits. A pattern that can fail belongs in `if let`, `let ... else` or `match`.
Matching a value moves a part that is not `Copy`, where destructuring in Python or Kotlin only adds names. Match a reference (`&opt`, `opt.as_ref()`) to borrow instead.
`_` ignores a part and does not move it. `_name` is a variable that does.

gotcha.title: Taking something apart that might not be there
gotcha.looks_fine: A `name=value` line splits into two halves, and you name both. It works for every line that has an `=`, and nothing in the code says what should happen for a line that has none.
gotcha.rust_sees: `split_once` returns an `Option`: `None` when the line has no `=`. A `let` pattern has to fit every value it can be given, and `Some((key, value))` does not fit `None`, so Rust refuses (E0005) and suggests `let ... else`.
gotcha.why: The line `mode` has no `=`. In the other languages the check for that is a step you can leave out, and nothing complains; the programs here leave it out and were run with that line: a wrong value, `undefined`, an exception, or a crash. Careful code checks (the layer-1 programs do), and C# 11's list pattern makes you. Rust makes the check part of the pattern, so leaving it out does not build.

go.says: `strings.Cut` returns a `found` flag, but `key, value, _ :=` throws it away; the layer-1 program keeps it with `if ...; found`. `go vet` accepts this version. For `mode` it prints `mode -> ` with an empty value and no error.

kotlin.says: `val (key, value) = line.split("=")` calls `component2()` on a list with one item, and throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.

typescript.says: TypeScript accepts this under `--strict`: `value` has type `string`, and at run time it is `undefined`, so the program prints `mode -> undefined`. The option `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, which `--strict` does not include, types `value` as `string | undefined` and then refuses `value.toUpperCase()`: the question Rust asks.

java.says: Java has no array pattern, so this indexes: `parts[1]` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` for the one-item array that `split` gives back.
java.out:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 1 out of bounds for length 1
	at Main.main(Main.java:5)

csharp.says: This indexes, it is not a pattern: `parts[1]` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`. C# 11's list pattern, `line.Split('=') is [var key, var value]`, has the shape of Rust's and is a test with an `else`, so it cannot crash.
csharp.out:
Unhandled exception. System.IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array.
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 5

c.says: `strchr` returns `NULL` when there is no `=`; the layer-1 program checks that, and this version leaves the check out, so `eq - line` and `eq + 1` are arithmetic on a null pointer. Undefined behaviour: on this machine the program died with a segmentation fault.

cpp.says: `find` returns `npos` when there is no `=` (the layer-1 program checks it; this version does not), and `npos + 1` wraps to 0, so the value half is the whole line. The program prints `mode -> mode` with no error.

from typing import NamedTuple


class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: int
    y: int


# unpacking is by position
x, y = Point(3, -2)
print(f"x = {x}, y = {y}")

for i, c in enumerate("abc"):
    print(f"{i}: {c}")

key, sep, value = "mode=fast".partition("=")
if sep:
    print(f"{key} -> {value}")

# * collects the items in the middle
first, *_, last = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(f"first = {first}, last = {last}")

unpack.py.code:
from typing import NamedTuple


class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: int
    y: int


# nested, with * for the rest of a sequence
(a, b), (c, d) = Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4)
head, *tail = [10, 20, 30]
print(f"a={a} b={b} c={c} d={d} head={head} tail={tail}")

# unpacking only gives the same objects second names: the source stays whole
point = Point(5, 6)
x, y = point
print(f"point is still {point}")

# a for loop unpacks each item
for name, (x, y) in {"p": Point(1, 2), "q": Point(3, 4)}.items():
    print(f"{name}: x={x} y={y}")
